caption: Figure 2: Diagram showing the different purposes of explainability in ML models sought by different audience profiles. Two goals occur to prevail across them: need for model understanding, and regulatory compliance. Image partly inspired by the one presented in [29], used with permission from IBM.
description:
This figure is a diagram illustrating the different purposes of explainability in machine learning (ML) models, as sought by various audience profiles. It shows how different groups, such as domain experts, users affected by model decisions, regulatory entities, data scientists, and managers, have distinct needs for understanding and compliance. The diagram highlights two overarching goals: the need for model understanding and regulatory compliance. It also includes a target audience section specifically for explainable artificial intelligence (XAI).

caption: Figure 3: Conceptual diagram exemplifying the different levels of transparency characterizing a ML model M ϕ , with ϕ denoting the parameter set of the model at hand: (a) simulatability; (b) decomposability; (c) algorithmic transparency. description:
This figure is a conceptual diagram illustrating different levels of transparency in machine learning models. It consists of three panels labeled (a), (b), and (c), each representing a different level of transparency: simulatability, decomposability, and algorithmic transparency, respectively. Panel (a) shows a model with a function g that combines outputs from functions fA and fB, leading to a decision rule based on the value of g. Panel (b) demonstrates a decision tree with rules based on input features x1, x2, and x3. Panel (c) presents a rule-based explanation derived from training data, showing that certain conditions on the input features lead to specific output decisions.

caption: Figure 6: Taxonomy of the reviewed literature and trends identified for explainability techniques related to different ML models. References boxed in blue, green and red correspond to XAI techniques using image, text or tabular data, respectively. In order to build this taxonomy, the literature has been analyzed in depth to discriminate whether a post-hoc technique can be seamlessly applied to any ML model, even if, e.g., explicitly mentions Deep Learning in its title and/or abstract.

The figure includes references to studies that use image, text, or tabular data.
